title: Seller Fallback Sentinel — Pocket Deck (sketch)
content:
Purpose: ultra-compact slide deck + speaker notes for platform sellers to handle canary and fallback conversations in a 5–7 minute field call.

Slide 1 — One-liner + why it matters
- One-liner: Redwood lets you keep customer apps online with predictable latency and graceful fallbacks when model or region capacity changes.
- Why mention at start: buyers panic about availability and sudden model regressions. This frames Redwood as reliability-first (not just cheaper tokens).
- Speaker note: start with a single sentence value prop, then ask: "Do you have soft-fail tolerances for your LLM features?"

Slide 2 — Common commercial triggers (3 bullets)
- Pilot blows past free-tier throughput and latency spikes appear.
- Customer requires an SLA/uptime guarantee for a core app flow (support, legal review).
- Capacity event: primary model overloaded or an upstream model version causes quality drift.
- Speaker note: connect each trigger to a tangible business risk (lost conversions, compliance alerts, or support load).

Slide 3 — How Redwood’s fallback story works (sketch)
- Routing policy: tiered routing (primary -> cheaper variant -> cached response -> fallback short answer).
- Canary rollouts: A/B route new model versions for % of traffic + automated quality checks.
- Graceful degrade: automated 503-to-fallback mapping with telemetry and customer alerts.
- Speaker note: keep it high level — emphasize control (you define fallbacks) and observability (you see the signal before it impacts users).

Slide 4 — Quick objection scripts (concise responses)
- Objection: "Fallbacks sound like degraded UX."
  Response: "Right, but they’re explicit and measured: we preserve core functionality and surface a small notice while we recover — far better than total outages. Also we can A/B test fallback wording and quality."
- Objection: "We can build this ourselves."
  Response: "You can, but you’ll spend months instrumenting routes, building rollbacks, and tuning costs. Redwood provides these primitives out of the box with telemetry tied to cost and quality."
- Objection: "How do you guarantee it won’t change model output semantics?"
  Response: "We use pinned model variants, small-model paraphrase checks, and regression alerts against your golden prompt set before increasing traffic to a new variant."

Slide 5 — Rapid field checklist (what to ask the customer)
- Which flows are revenue-critical (list top 3)?
- Current 95th and 99th percentile latencies for those flows? (or proxy QPS/peak concurrency)
- Acceptable failure mode: stale cache vs simplified fallback vs offline message?
- Compliance constraints (data residency / on-prem needs)?
- Speaker note: these answers map directly to routing policies and SLA tiers.

Slide 6 — Technical callouts sellers can use (single-sentence tech bullets)
- Redis-backed prefix cache reduces common token cost and avoids extra model calls for repeated prompts.
- Canary ingress allows 1–10% traffic ramp with automated quality checks on your eval set.
- Multi-region routing ensures traffic shifts without manual DNS changes.
- Token-level cost breakdown visible in Console for immediate tradeoff decisions.

Slide 7 — Mini case: ecommerce support bot (2-paragraph sketch)
- Problem: support chat went down during Black Friday surge; fallback to static KB lost revenue and increased hold times.
- Redwood approach: configured a two-tier policy (primary L) + quantized mid-tier (faster, cheaper) + cached answers for top 200 intents. Canaryed a model upgrade earlier in the week and rolled back automatically at 2% misclassification. Result: 98.9% uptime for support flows, 40% cut in per-conversation inference cost during peak.
- Speaker note: use this story when the buyer cares about peak-day reliability.

Slide 8 — Hand-raise moments and next steps (seller play)
- Hand-raise signals: they mention SLAs, Black Friday / peak events, or a need for private deployments.
- Next steps: 1) Quick infra triage call (15 min) to capture latency/QPS, 2) propose a canary plan + cost snapshot, 3) 30-day pilot with reserved capacity option.

Slide 9 — Appendix: 30-second technical deep-dive bullets for eng stakeholders
- Runtime selects attention kernels by seq-len distribution; this avoids a single slow path for long queries.
- KV cache and prefix cache reduce re-computation across sessions and multi-turn dialogs.
- Autoscaling with spillover routing: extra traffic is routed to cheaper variants rather than dropped.

Slide 10 — Quick FAQ + metrics to share (copyable lines)
- "We target P99 inference latency <= 500ms for reserved capacity tiers; hosted varies by model size."
- "Canary length: typical is 24–72 hours or until eval coverage hits 10k requests."
- "Fallback types: cached, paraphrase-with-clarity, minimal-answer, and offline-banner."

Appendix — quick templates for email follow-ups (copy/paste)
- Subject: Canary plan + quick infra triage notes
- Body: Hi <name>, thanks for the sync — as discussed I captured your top flows (X, Y, Z), current P95/P99 and suggested two-tier policy: primary = model-A, fallback = quantized-B + answer-cache for top 200 intents. Proposed next: 15-min infra triage. Cheers, <you>

Draft notes / TODOs
- Convert slides into a 6-slide PDF for SDRs (this is just speaker-notes heavy).
- Get an approved case number / redacted metrics from customer success for the ecommerce example.
- Add small diagram (routing map) and attach Console screenshots showing fallback telemetry.
- Sync with product on exact P99 numbers for dedicated tiers before finalizing public deck.

Tone: conversational, seller-friendly, not too technical — but includes a short technical appendix for eng buyers.

---
History: created during a field enablement sprint to give sellers a lightweight, repeatable framing to reduce time-to-proposal on fallback/availability conversations.
